title: The Central Government: Chancellery, Secretariat, and Six Ministries
description: An editorial introduction to The Central Government: Chancellery, Secretariat, and Six Ministries, part of the expanding KOREA history archive.

blocks.title: Governing through written work
paragraphs: Central institutions in Goryeo adapted established East Asian bureaucratic patterns while responding to the monarchy's particular political environment. Secretariats and ministries could receive proposals, prepare decisions, transmit instructions, and record personnel or fiscal matters. These tasks gave written administration a central place in royal government, but documents alone could not ensure compliance. The court relied on trained officials and relationships with local actors to translate policy into practical action.

blocks.title: Offices and personal networks
paragraphs: An office created a formal responsibility, while family background, education, patrons, and factional relationships could influence its holder's career. The tension between institutional ideal and social reality is crucial to understanding Goryeo government. Officials were not simply interchangeable technicians: they belonged to households and elite networks whose interests sometimes conflicted. Studying rank and appointment alongside political disputes shows how a bureaucracy could strengthen monarchy and still provide arenas for aristocratic competition.

blocks.title: Information had to travel
paragraphs: A central court needed reports about harvests, taxes, law, and provincial conditions. Each report passed through people who selected what to communicate. Delays, local disputes, and imperfect records limited what rulers knew. A broad narrative of institutions should therefore examine roads, messengers, clerks, and documentary routines, not merely formal charts of ministries. Administrative power depends on information as much as on command.
